editor_spans.body: Andy Burnham's line on the long-term EU relationship is the most important thing he said in his Commons statement on 12 October, and he placed it after the Ukraine and Middle East sections, where it was easy to miss. Over the last ten years every Prime Minister has treated the Brexit settlement as closed and argued only about the details. Burnham is now calling it a 'status quo' that is 'not good enough' and saying it would be 'a major dereliction of duty' to avoid discussing it.

The order of steps matters. First comes the 20 November Brussels summit, with its trade deal on food and drink, its emissions-trading deal and its youth scheme. After that comes 'a serious dialogue about the different options'. Saying the public 'will be the boss' is how politicians prepare the ground for a referendum without promising one. This is a gradual approach: each sector-by-sector deal is presented as relief for farmers and exporters, and together the deals build a case that the current arrangement costs money. The examples of salmon checks, seed potatoes and 1,400-pound shipment costs make that case without anyone having to say so.

'A decade of drift and division' dates the problem to 2016 without naming the referendum. Pair it with 'Britain is back' and the speech becomes an argument about the Brexit years, not a report on the UN General Assembly.

Over four days the government's position on the energy ceasefire changed sharply. On 12 October the Prime Minister welcomed Trump's 'reciprocal energy ceasefire' and said Ukraine would implement it once a start date was set. By 14 October, Downing Street was describing Russia's 'blatant indiscriminate attacks' on energy infrastructure since Trump made his call, and saying Russia 'had no interest in peace'. The ceasefire Britain welcomed seems to have produced nothing.

Britain's interest was never only about Ukraine. Burnham tied the energy ceasefire to getting diesel 'back onto world markets'. The government's 10 October response to the US–Russia agreement turned quickly to energy prices and the cost of living. Healey talks about conflict in the Middle East and Europe 'hitting people across the world'. Meanwhile Britain is flying refuelling missions over Saudi Arabia as the Houthis attack its airports. The underlying pressure is two wars squeezing fuel supply. That explains why London welcomes a US-brokered deal it cannot shape, and why it keeps saying it 'fully supports US-led efforts' even when those efforts fail.

The numbers are smaller than the language. 'Doubles down' amounts to £45 million of missiles, of which only £10 million is being brought forward for winter, against a £1.6 billion programme already committed over four years. The new commitments are requests to ministers to 'draw up' packages and appeals to partners to copy the LNG ban. That is Britain coordinating other countries' support more than adding much of its own.

Burnham's offer to Holyrood is the metro-mayor model he ran in Greater Manchester, now applied to Scotland. In Scotland, though, local government is devolved, so Westminster cannot hand powers to Scottish regions on its own. That is why it is framed as an 'offer' and an 'invitation'. Calling the Scottish Government 'one of the most centralised devolved administrations in Europe' moves the centralisation charge from London to Edinburgh. If the First Minister refuses, Labour can present the SNP as the side holding power back from Fife and the Highlands. The real aim is to compete for Scottish voters' loyalty, with No10 North and the Scotland Office as the tools.

Derby's GBR headquarters is due to open in spring 2029, about when the next general election is expected. Until then the gains in this announcement are promises. The 'hundreds of jobs' are an office for up to 450 staff, mostly moved from elsewhere rather than newly created, and building does not begin until 2027. The figure that explains the policy appears late in the release: under 7% of railway workers are under 25. The industry's workforce is ageing, and 600 apprentices over four years is a small response to that.

County Tyrone's new Lord-Lieutenant was the RUC District Commander in Omagh on the day of the 1998 bombing. The official notice includes this as a career detail. However, there is a public inquiry into the bombing, which, as I understand it, is examining whether the state could have prevented the attack. If so, the policing of Omagh at that time is exactly what is under examination. Making the officer in charge that day the King's representative in the county, while the inquiry is still running, is a choice that families of the victims may read differently from the Palace.
